---
title: "Natural history of aneurysmal SAH"
---

::: {.npr-disclaimer}
Educational overview. DRAFT — see [Sources](sources.qmd). Phases overlap on purpose: a
thick-clot, poor-grade patient stays in the DCI window past day 14.
:::

The tool organizes SAH around a **time × system matrix**. Time is *day post-ictus* (day of
hemorrhage = day 0), with a secondary clock of *day post-securing* for blood-pressure
liberalization and VTE prophylaxis. The systems: rebleeding, hydrocephalus/EVD/ICP,
DCI/vasospasm, sodium/volume, cardiopulmonary, fever/infection, seizure, hematologic
(anemia/VTE), and cognition/mood/disposition.

## The five phases

### Phase 1 — Hyperacute / pre-securing (day 0–1)

The aneurysm is not yet secured. Everything is organized around **preventing rebleeding**
(highest risk in the first 24 h, high mortality): titratable blood-pressure control, pain and
stimulation control, reversal of anticoagulation, and securing the aneurysm as early as
feasible. Treat acute obstructive hydrocephalus with an EVD, but avoid aggressive CSF drainage
before the aneurysm is secured. Expect cardiopulmonary stunning — troponin bump, QTc changes,
non-coronary wall-motion abnormality, neurogenic pulmonary edema. Grade the patient
(WFNS/Hunt-Hess, modified Fisher). Start nimodipine. The seizure-prophylaxis decision is made
here — a short course or none, and not phenytoin.

### Phase 2 — Early post-securing (day 1–4)

Aneurysm secured. Blood-pressure goals **liberalize** — the target becomes euvolemia, *not*
prophylactic hypervolemia. Sodium starts to drift. Establish the DCI-surveillance cadence:
hourly exams, a baseline TCD, an agreed imaging plan. Begin pharmacologic VTE prophylaxis a set
interval after securing. In poor-grade patients, set up multimodal monitoring (cEEG, PbtO2).

### Phase 3 — DCI window (day 4–14, peak ~6–9)

**Delayed cerebral ischemia** is the dominant threat. Detect it: hourly exam for a new focal
deficit or a drop in consciousness; TCD trends; CT perfusion/CTA when the exam changes; cEEG
(alpha-delta ratio) and PbtO2 in the patient too poor-grade to examine. Treat it: exclude the
mimics (seizure, hydrocephalus, hyponatremia, sedation, fever), then **induced hypertension**
first with a bedside response check, endovascular rescue (IA vasodilators, angioplasty) if
refractory. "Triple-H" is obsolete — hemodilution and prophylactic hypervolemia are out. The
sodium nadir and the fever peak fall in this window; keep the hemoglobin higher than the usual
restrictive ICU trigger while DCI risk is active.

### Phase 4 — Resolution (day 10–21)

Vasospasm risk recedes (later in thick-clot / poor-grade patients). Nimodipine **finishes at
day 21**. Begin the EVD wean — raise the level or clamp, watch exam / ICP / ventricle size; a
failed wean means a VP shunt. Shunt dependence is common after IVH, poor grade, and older age —
set expectations with the family early. Mobilize; start rehab planning.

### Phase 5 — Recovery / pre-discharge (day 14–30+)

Shunt if the wean failed. Taper any AED if the patient is seizure-free. **Name the cognitive,
executive, and mood sequelae explicitly** — depression, anxiety, PTSD, and fatigue are common
even after good motor recovery, and a patient who walks out the door can still have disabling
executive dysfunction. Arrange follow-up vascular imaging (coil surveillance). Counsel secondary
prevention: smoking cessation, blood-pressure control, and familial screening when criteria are
met.
